text: A studio executive rejects scripts for a living, which means the threat now arriving in his mail could have come from any of the writers he has already forgotten. Robert Altman builds the film out of that problem, and the joke is that identifying the sender matters less than the fact that the hunted man is also the man who decides what gets made. The suspense keeps sliding sideways into lunches, pitches and green lights, where the film is happiest. Comedy, thriller and mystery share the 124 minutes without any of them winning. Hollywood then gave it prizes for direction, editing and the adapted screenplay, which is its own kind of punchline. What lingers is the temperature: a business filmed by someone who knows exactly how a rejection travels, and how far it carries.

Thirty-six hours in Los Angeles, and a cast arranged so that every person in it will eventually collide with someone they would cross the street to avoid. Paul Haggis writes for collision — a district attorney and his wife, a shopkeeper, two policemen, two carjackers, a Korean couple — and cuts between them at a rate that keeps the design visible at every moment. The city on screen is one the story treats as still braced after September 11, where everyone arrives at every encounter already carrying an assumption. Nothing anybody says is softened. Whether coincidence at this density reveals a city or only stages one is the question the method leaves open, and the Academy answered it by handing the film best picture. 112 minutes, and none of them cool down.

In 1937 an American studio released a picture whose hero is a French novelist who accused his own country's army of framing an innocent man. The first half is a rise: Zola makes his name writing about the parts of Paris that respectable readers preferred not to hear about, then settles into an upper-class calm. The second half spends that calm. A Jewish officer is imprisoned as a spy, and a writer with a comfortable life has to decide what a reputation is for. William Dieterle follows the fictionalised life as far as the libel charge, so the film cares less about what Zola wrote than about what it cost him to put his name on it. Private rooms and public case occupy the same 116 minutes, and the weight shifts steadily toward the second.

The house on the pond opens for another summer, and the two people who have been coming to it for decades arrive with the old argument packed alongside the luggage. Norman and Ethel Thayer have worked out a peace between themselves; their daughter Chelsea has never managed one with her father. Mark Rydell keeps the scale small — one season, one shoreline, a handful of rooms — so the pressure comes from timing rather than incident. The recognitions fall where the work is: the two lead performances, and photography asked to make water and changing light hold a summer's worth of mood. What is at stake is not a crisis but a last chance, and nobody in the family will name it directly. The warmth in this film is real, and it is not free.

Hortense buries the woman who raised her, then goes looking for the one who did not. What she finds is not a secret waiting to be exposed but a person: Cynthia, white, working class, unprepared, her life already crowded with people who want something from her. Mike Leigh gives the encounter 142 minutes, and the length is the argument, since the film sits in kitchens and cafés while two women who cannot be to each other what the word mother implies work out whether they can be anything at all. Nothing is heightened. Scenes run well past the point they have made, and embarrassment does the job that plot does elsewhere. Los Angeles critics named it their best picture of the year, and the choice makes sense: these are performances that seem to be happening rather than delivered.

Juliane keeps visiting her sister in prison and disagrees with her the entire time. Both are a priest's daughters, both wanted the country changed; one went into journalism, the other into an armed group, and now one is in isolation and the other is her only contact with the world. Margarethe von Trotta puts the argument in the visiting room, where the political question shrinks into a practical one about who keeps turning up. The German title, Die bleierne Zeit, names a heaviness rather than an event, which suits a film made in 1981 about 1968, close enough to both to be uncomfortable. It came away with the Golden Lion and Germany's award for best feature. What holds after the politics is the sibling arrangement: loyalty and disapproval performed as one act, on a schedule, under supervision.

A rumour empties a town in 1944: the Germans mean to blow it up, the Americans are close, and a group of Italians walk into the fields on nothing but what they have heard. Paolo Taviani sets that walk on the night of San Lorenzo, when folklore says wishes are granted, and lets the two things share the same wheat. Nobody has reliable information. The party divides along lines of belief rather than politics, and the film stays with the walkers for its 105 minutes, so the war arrives the way it arrives for civilians, as noise from elsewhere that is abruptly here. Cannes gave it the Grand Prix and Italy's David di Donatello named it the year's film, but what stays is the texture of a countryside crossed on foot by people guessing.

By the 1890s the trade these two men are in is disappearing underneath them, and the plan they settle on — leave the continent altogether — is less an escape than an admission. George Roy Hill spends much of the film on talk, two professionals working out logistics while the country that needed their line of work finishes closing. The posse behind them is never given a face, which turns pursuit into something closer to weather: constant, unarguable, indifferent. It is also, very often, funny. The Academy cited the photography and the score, a fair reading of a picture that travels on landscape and rhythm as much as on incident, and AFI later placed it among a hundred American films. Underneath the charm the subject is obsolescence: what a man does when he is expert at something his country has stopped needing.

Christmas of 1183, and a king with three sons and no named heir gathers the whole family under one roof for the holiday. Henry II wants John; Eleanor wants Richard; everyone at the table has calculated what the others will do and is wrong about at least one of them. Anthony Harvey films it as a chamber piece with a kingdom for stakes, 134 minutes of talk in cold rooms, where a compliment is a manoeuvre and affection is genuine and gets used anyway. The costume award describes the surface. The two acting citations describe where the picture lives, which is in the pauses between lines sharpened until they cut. History supplies the map; the film is watching a marriage wage war with the only weapons it has left.

A politician is killed in the street during a demonstration, and within the hour the official account is tidier than what happened. Costa-Gavras runs everything after that as procedure: one magistrate, a pile of statements that will not agree, an army and a government with every reason to keep the file shut. The film moves at the speed of its cutting, and the editing award is not decoration but method, evidence assembled in front of an audience faster than the authorities can bury it. An Algerian production shot in French and released in 1969, it declines to treat the state as a villain and shows instead men protecting their own careers, which is worse and much harder to beat. 122 minutes with the shape of a case file read aloud by someone in a hurry.

A diving accident took everything below Ramón Sampedro's neck and none of his capacity to argue. He was a ship mechanic who wrote poetry on the side, and he spent thirty years pressing for the legal right to end his own life. Alejandro Amenábar keeps close to the household that grew around that fight: a lawyer named Julia, a friend named Rosa, both of them arguing with him and both of them coming back. The camera's problem is how to hold a man who cannot move without reducing him to that stillness, and the answer runs through the room, the sea beyond it, and a voice doing what the body cannot. The lead performance collected a Volpi Cup and a European award, the film a Goya, but the 126 minutes ask for something harder than agreement.

Marrying the factory owner's daughter is a faster route up than any promotion, and the young accountant who works this out does the sum without flinching. The edge is that the calculation never gets dressed as romance: he is allowed to want money and position plainly, and is then complicated by a married woman he had not planned on loving. Class is not atmosphere here but currency — which house a man may enter, which match counts as good, what an accent costs him in an office. Jack Clayton keeps the tone dry and the sympathy unstable. The Academy's citations went to the two leads, which is right, since 115 minutes of ambition working on a face is the actual event. The BFI keeps it on its list of British films; it stays a hard picture about wanting.

Two things hold at once: Vera Drake believes she is helping, and 1950s Britain calls what she does a crime. Mike Leigh gives the first long stretch of the film to ordinary domestic time — tea, work, small kindnesses handed over without ceremony — so that everything arriving after it carries weight. The interest is never in whether the law will notice. It is in the distance between what Vera thinks she is doing and the word the state keeps for it, and in a family that has lived alongside that distance without once seeing it. The Golden Lion went to the film, the Volpi Cup to its lead. No one here is caricatured, the officials included. 125 minutes, mostly in small rooms, and the temperature drops so gradually it is hard to say when.

A man who can win any duel and write any line refuses to say the one sentence that would cost him something. Cyrano loves his cousin Roxane, has decided in advance that his face disqualifies him, and finds a route to her that runs through another man's mouth — a scheme with the shape of a comedy and the mechanics of self-injury. Jean-Paul Rappeneau plays it at full period scale, 137 minutes with the swords, the crowds and the tailoring intact, and the costume award is no footnote: the subject is surfaces and who is permitted to be looked at. The César for best film went to it, and the Academy cited the lead performance. The talk comes fast, overlapping, competitive, and the wit works as armour a long time before it works as charm.
